candidates.label: Ancient Agora of Athens
candidates.support: The excavated civic square just north of the Acropolis is identified as Athens's ancient marketplace (agora); the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places Paul's daily reasoning with those who met him there, including Stoic philosophers, in this marketplace, distinct from his reasoning with the Jews and devout persons in the synagogue, and locates the Painted Portico in and around this square. Acts 17:18 adds that Epicurean philosophers were also among those who reasoned with him there.

summary.text: The Agora was the civic and commercial square of ancient Athens, lying just north of the Acropolis and ringed by porticoes (stoas). According to Acts, Paul reasoned there every day with whoever happened to meet him, drawing the attention of Epicurean and Stoic philosophers who then brought him to the nearby Areopagus.

history.text: The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes Paul passing the Ceramicus and the "Theseum" on his way to the Agora (Market-Place), just north of the Acropolis, noting that porticoes (stoas) stood in and around it, among them the Painted Portico (Stoa Poecile) where Paul met the successors of the philosopher Zeno, the Stoics, and disputed with them daily.
Today the excavated site of the Agora lies north-west of the Acropolis.

scripture.textWEB: So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the marketplace every day with those who met him.

politicalHistory.note: The Roman biographer Suetonius: on his departure from Greece, the emperor Nero "presented the entire province with freedom."

The Roman biographer Suetonius records that the emperor Vespasian "made provinces of Achaia, Lycia, Rhodes, Byzantium and Samos, taking away their freedom," but gives no year for this, so the status here is shown as unclear from Vespasian's first full year as emperor until his death in 79, when it is a province again.
